comparisons.peer_topic: Use of Credit Default Protection for Hedging
comparisons.peer_summary: The company purchases credit protection to cover funded and unfunded portions of certain credit exposures and may sell protection within industry or counterparty groups to lower costs. At December 31, 2024, net notional credit default protection purchased was $10.4 billion, compared to $10.9 billion at the end of 2023.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and BAC disclose the use of purchased credit protection (CDS) to hedge specific credit exposures, which impacts their respective risk metrics. JPM notes that 'credit protection purchased against certain retained loans' is included in its VaR, while BAC states it 'purchases credit protection to cover the funded portion as well as the unfunded portion of certain credit exposures' and reports net notional amounts ($10.4 billion in 2024). JPM's disclosure links this protection directly to the VaR calculation components and presentation updates, whereas BAC's disclosure focuses on the hedging strategy and notional volume.

sentences.text: (c)Includes the derivative CVA, hedges of the CVA and credit protection purchased against certain retained loans and lending-related commitments, which are reported in principal transactions revenue.
We purchase credit protection to cover the funded portion as well as the unfunded portion of certain credit exposures.

At December 31, 2024 and 2023, net notional credit default protection purchased in our credit derivatives portfolio to hedge our funded and unfunded exposures for which we elected the fair value option, as well as certain other credit exposures, was $10.4 billion and $10.9 billion.

comparisons.peer_summary: The credit portfolio comprises mark-to-market positions from non-trading business units, CVA for derivative counterparties, associated CVA hedges, market sensitivity FVA hedges, and hedges of the loan portfolio, fair value option loans, and leveraged finance pipeline, excluding FVA and DVA.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Citi explicitly include Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) and associated CVA hedges in their Credit Portfolio VaR. JPM states that its VaR 'includes the derivative CVA, hedges of the CVA... and credit protection purchased against certain retained loans', while Citi's credit portfolio is 'composed of... the CVA relating to derivative counterparties, all associated CVA hedges'. A key difference is that Citi explicitly excludes FVA and DVA from this component, whereas JPM's disclosure focuses on the inclusion of CVA and credit protection, noting that CVA components for specific counterparties were removed due to widened spreads.

sentences.text: (c)Includes the derivative CVA, hedges of the CVA and credit protection purchased against certain retained loans and lending-related commitments, which are reported in principal transactions revenue.

In line with the Firm's internal model governance, the credit risk component of CVA related to certain counterparties was removed from Credit Portfolio VaR due to the widening of the credit spreads for those counterparties to elevated levels.

(4) The credit portfolio is composed of mark-to-market positions associated with non-trading business units, the CVA relating to derivative counterparties, all associated CVA hedges and market sensitivity FVA hedges.
FVA and DVA are not included.

comparisons.peer_summary: The VaR measure excludes positions not accounted for at fair value (such as held-to-maturity securities and amortized cost loans/deposits), available-for-sale securities with unrealized gains/losses in other comprehensive income, positions best measured by sensitivity measures, and the impact of credit spread changes on derivatives and liabilities where the fair value option was elected.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and Goldman Sachs explicitly exclude retained loan portfolios or loans accounted for at amortized cost from their VaR measures because they are not reported at fair value. JPM states, 'This VaR does not include the retained loan portfolio, which is not reported at fair value,' while GS notes VaR does not include 'Positions that are not accounted for at fair value, such as held-to-maturity securities and loans... that are accounted for at amortized cost'. Unlike JPM, which highlights the exclusion of retained loans in the context of CVA/hedge inclusions, GS provides a broader list of exclusions including available-for-sale securities and credit spread impacts.
